extracted.intended_audience: writers and illustrators creating a one-page graphic novel for young girls
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for designing and producing a single-page graphic novel aimed at little girls, covering story idea selection, panel layout, dialogue/captions, character/background art, inking/coloring, lettering, and (optional) SVG rendering constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: SVG shape usage / avoid quadratic curves
rubrics_metrics.description: In the SVG use shapes like ellipses, triangles etc and polygons but try to defer from using quadratic curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing SVG code for the image, favor basic primitives (ellipses, triangles, polygons, rectangles, lines). The page explicitly asks to create SVG code using these shapes and to avoid quadratic curve commands; this implies constructing letter/object shapes with polygons/paths composed of straight segments where possible. (No scoring guidance beyond this constraint.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate letters into objects (letter-object fusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine alphabet letters and objects so parts of the object form the letter shape (e.g., elephant trunk shaped like J; house roof forming an A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design objects so a recognizable part of the object doubles as the letter—examples provided: elephant trunk as J, house roof as A, pig tail shaped like H, house roof shaped like U, chair backrest shaped like K, dog tail shaped like Q, car front grill shaped like E. Keep both the object identity and the letter shape legible. Use this technique as a motif for classes of examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch panel layout according to narrative flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch a rough layout of the page, dividing it into panels of different sizes and shapes according to the flow of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a large panel for the opening scene (establishing shot) and a large final panel for the ending; use smaller panels for intermediate beats (finding the crayon, drawing the unicorn, seeing it come to life). Vary panel sizes and shapes to guide pacing and emphasis. The layout should reflect emotional and narrative beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write simple, expressive dialogue and captions
rubrics_metrics.description: Write dialogue and captions for each panel using simple and expressive language that matches the story's tone and mood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use captions to introduce characters/setting and short speech lines to show curiosity, desire, and joy. Example speech: "Wow, what a cool crayon!", "I wish I had a unicorn friend", "You're real!" Include onomatopoeic sound effects (e.g., "Scribble, scribble", "Poof!", "Neigh!") to add drama and humor. Keep sentences short and age-appropriate for young children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character & background design appropriate for young girls
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw characters and backgrounds using a clear, colorful style that appeals to little girls (e.g., cute, expressive girl; majestic friendly unicorn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the protagonist visually appealing: big eyes, expressive features, long hair, a dress. Make secondary characters charming (unicorn with horn, mane, tail). Add small personal details and accessories to make characters unique and interesting (flower in hair, star on unicorn forehead, poster on the wall). Backgrounds should be clear and colorful but not cluttered—support the narrative and mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inking and coloring conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ink and color the panels using clear outlines and bright, appealing colors, with shading and highlights for depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use black ink for outlines and bright colors (suggestions: pink, purple, blue) for characters and backgrounds. Apply shading, highlights, and simple patterns to create depth and contrast—examples include a gradient for the sky, sparkles to indicate magic, or stripes on the unicorn's coat. Choose coloring techniques that read well at the small scale of a single-page comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lettering, fonts, and text placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Add dialogue and captions with a font or lettering style that fits the story's voice, and place them in balloons/boxes that match panel shapes and sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select lettering styles that reinforce tone: e.g., a round, bubbly font for the girl's speech and an elegant/script font for captions. Place text in speech balloons and caption boxes sized and shaped for the panel. Use typographic emphasis (bold, italic, larger size, different color or balloon shape) to stress key words or emotions. Ensure legibility and that text does not obscure critical artwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify concept for a single-page execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a very simple, focused storyline that can be resolved on one page (e.g., a girl who draws a unicorn that comes to life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a single central event and a small number of beats so the story fits cleanly into one page. Reduce subplots and secondary conflicts; focus on clear, emotionally satisfying beginning, middle, and end within limited panels. The page suggests reducing complexity ("let’s make it even simpler") as good practice for one-page comics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sound effects and pacing devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ sound effects and panel pacing to add drama and humor and to communicate action succinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include short onomatopoeia (e.g., "Scribble, scribble", "Poof!", "Neigh!") sized and styled to match the action. Arrange panel sizes and sequencing to control pacing—larger panels slow the reader for important moments, smaller panels speed through quick actions.
